夜鶯琴源自日本 taishogoto，1930年代傳入南亞，在印度與巴基斯坦流行: The bulbul tarang comes from the Japanese taishogoto, which reached South Asia in the 1930s and became popular in India and Pakistan as a standard instrument, also called the Indian banjo. The present form has 14 strings in three groups: 2 main strings (melody and bass), 4 jhala strings and 8 swarmandal strings; above the fretboard are typewriter-like keys which, when pressed, shorten the string and raise the pitch. Similar instruments are called akkordolia in Germany and Austria, benju in Pakistan, kottafoshi in the Maldives, and medolin among the Indian community of Fiji; there is also a more complex, electrified shahi baaja. Well-known players include Hala Strana, the jazz group Air and Ahuva Ozeri of Tel Aviv.

The strings are of steel wire or a copper alloy, which keeps the pitch stable and the string durable. The keys and mechanism are metal, usually brass or steel, so that the string pitch can be controlled precisely. Leather or sheepskin may be used inside the resonator as a tone-adjusting material. The whole structure joins the warmth of wood to the acoustic penetration of metal.

Its range is wide and richly layered, from the deep, heavy bass strings to the high, sharp melody strings. The many-string design gives the main strings the melody while the jhala and swarmandal strings supply harmony and overtones, so the sound flows in waves. Against the sharp, piercing banjo the bulbul tarang is warmer and softer; against the meditative harp it carries more penetration. The design of the resonator keeps the brilliance of a metal instrument while retaining the warmth of a string instrument, and the overall sound has a strongly fused East Asian and South Asian character.

The bulbul tarang, also called the Indian banjo, is a chordophone from India, developed from the Japanese taishōgoto and perhaps brought to South Asia in the 1930s. The present form has fourteen strings in three groups: two main melody and bass strings, four jhala strings and eight swarmandal strings; the strings cross the Surpatti fretboard, above which are typewriter-like keys that stop or shorten the string to raise the pitch. It is usually played with the bow or with a plectrum, and chords can be selected as on an autoharp; it is mostly used to accompany singing, and it was once popular in both India and Pakistan.
